name: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for chronic pain (ACT)
founders: Steven C. Hayes (with Kirk Strosahl, Kelly Wilson)
founded_year_range: ACT origins early 1980s ('comprehensive distancing'); manual 1999; chronic-pain application 2005 (Dahl, Wilson, Luciano & Hayes, Context Press; McCracken, IASP Press); ACBS formed 2005; Stanza app (Swing Therapeutics) FDA De Novo DEN220083, 9 May 2023
cost_summary: Non-proprietary model, free to use. US clinician delivery is roughly USD 100-250 per session (~USD 800-2,500 for 8-12 sessions out of pocket; typical market range, estimate), usually insurance-covered. Free at point of use in NHS pain services. Self-help books ~USD 15-25. Stanza (Swing Therapeutics) requires a prescription and is offered through clinical partners in 8 US states; no price is published (checked Swing's Stanza page and coverage news, Oct 2026). Highmark covers it for commercial members in PA, WV, DE and NY. Swing was acquired by XRHealth in July 2026.
mechanisms: psychological inflexibility / experiential avoidance (ACT hexaflex; Relational Frame Theory)
mechanism_summary: ACT attributes disability and suffering in chronic pain mainly to psychological inflexibility rather than to pain itself. The components are experiential avoidance and control efforts, cognitive fusion with pain-related thoughts, and a narrowing of behaviour away from valued activities. The theory rests on Relational Frame Theory, a behavioural account of language. ACT makes no claim that pain is brain-generated or reversible and no aetiological claims about specific syndromes. The goal is valued living with pain; pain reduction is a by-product. Mediation evidence is mixed: psychological inflexibility mediated outcomes in Wicksell 2013 and Kemani 2016, and acceptance did so in Simister 2018, but 4 of 5 path models showed no mediation in EFFIGACT (Luciano 2014).
techniques: creative hopelessness (reviewing costs of pain-control attempts)
committed action / graded values-based activity and exposure
mainstream_notes: NICE NG193 (April 2021), recommendation 1.2.3, says to consider ACT or CBT for chronic primary pain in people aged 16 and over (verified). ACBS reports that these were the only psychological therapies NICE recommended. NICE NG155 (2020) also lists ACT as an option for tinnitus. APA Division 12 rated ACT for chronic pain 'Strong' under its original EST criteria, but its page now lists the treatment as pending re-evaluation under the 2015 criteria. ACT is a core model in NHS specialist pain services such as the Bath Centre for Pain Services (still running national programmes at the RUH in 2026). VA trials exist, and VA stepped-care clinics run ACT groups; the early Vowles & Sorrell manual (2007) came from Bath/VA Palo Alto, but no official VA-published ACT-for-pain manual was found. Swing Therapeutics' ACT app Stanza received FDA De Novo authorization (DEN220083) on 9 May 2023, the first for fibromyalgia symptoms. XRHealth acquired Swing Therapeutics in July 2026.
insurance_notes: In the US, licensed clinicians bill ACT under standard psychotherapy and health-behaviour CPT codes (90832-90837, 96156-96159); there is no ACT-specific code. In the UK it is NHS-funded. Stanza needs a prescription and is offered via clinical partners (Swing Care, Southwest Medical, UPMC); Highmark covers it for commercial members in PA, WV, DE and NY (Feb 2025). Medicare does not (as of Jul 2026), and CMS DMHT codes G0552-G0554 cover only 21 CFR 882.5801/882.5803 devices, not Stanza (882.5804). Partner clinics bill insurers for the clinical visits. No price is published.

key_trials.citation: Gendreau RM, McCracken LM, Williams DA, Luciano JV et al. Lancet 2024;404:364-374 (PROSPER-FM)
key_trials.design: Phase 3 multicentre RCT (25 US sites), 12-wk self-guided smartphone ACT (Stanza) vs active symptom-tracking/education control; funded by Swing Therapeutics; research staff unmasked
key_trials.finding: PGIC responders 71% vs 22% (difference 48.4%, 95% CI 37.9-58.9); no device-related adverse events

key_trials.citation: Catella S, Gendreau RM et al. J Behav Med 2024;47:27-42 (SMART-FM)
key_trials.design: Phase 2 RCT, digital ACT vs digital symptom tracking, fibromyalgia; retrospectively registered
key_trials.finding: PGIC improved 73% vs 22% (p<.001); FIQ-R between-arm d=0.44 (p=.074, n.s.)

key_trials.design: RCT, group ACT vs pregabalin+duloxetine vs waitlist, fibromyalgia (Spain)
key_trials.finding: ACT superior to drugs and waitlist on FIQ; medium effects maintained at 6 months; 4 of 5 mediation models null

key_trials.design: RCT, 8-session group ACT vs CBT, chronic pain (primary-care-oriented protocols, VA)
key_trials.finding: Both improved; no between-group differences on any outcome; higher satisfaction with ACT

key_trials.citation: Kemani MK, Olsson GL, Lekander M, Hesser H, Andersson E, Wicksell RK. Clin J Pain 2015;31:1004-1016
key_trials.design: RCT, 12-session group ACT vs applied relaxation (active comparator), longstanding pain
key_trials.finding: Both improved; ACT reduced disability faster, AR caught up by 6 months; ~20% clinically significant change; ACT more cost-effective only to 3 months

key_trials.citation: Wicksell RK et al. Eur J Pain 2013;17:599-611
key_trials.design: RCT, 12-session group ACT vs waitlist, fibromyalgia (women)
key_trials.finding: ACT improved pain-related functioning, FM impact, depression and anxiety; mediated by psychological inflexibility

key_trials.citation: Wicksell RK, Melin L, Lekander M, Olsson GL. Pain 2009;141:248-257
key_trials.design: RCT, exposure/acceptance-based ACT (~10 sessions) vs multidisciplinary treatment incl. amitriptyline, paediatric longstanding pain
key_trials.finding: ACT better on functioning, pain intensity and discomfort when follow-ups were included (ITT)

key_trials.citation: Lin J et al. Dtsch Arztebl Int 2017;114:681-688 (ACTonPain)
key_trials.design: RCT, guided vs unguided internet ACT vs waitlist
key_trials.finding: Guided ACT d=0.58 on pain interference (NNT 3.14); unguided not significant on primary outcome

key_trials.citation: Trompetter HR et al. J Behav Med 2015;38:66-80
key_trials.design: RCT, internet ACT vs expressive writing vs waitlist
key_trials.finding: At 3-month follow-up, d=0.47 vs expressive writing on interference; not significant vs waitlist (p=.11); 48% adherence

key_trials.citation: Simister HD et al. J Pain 2018;19:741-753
key_trials.design: RCT, online ACT+TAU vs TAU, fibromyalgia
key_trials.finding: Large effect on FM impact (reported d 1.26 post, 1.59 at 3 months); mediated by pain acceptance

key_trials.citation: Herbert MS et al. J Pain 2017;18:200-211
key_trials.design: Noninferiority RCT, video-telehealth vs in-person 8-week ACT, veterans

key_trials.citation: Williams ACC, Fisher E, Hearn L, Eccleston C. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;8:CD007407
key_trials.finding: No clear difference vs active control at treatment end; all ACT evidence very low quality

key_trials.citation: Lai L, Liu Y, McCracken LM, Li Y, Ren Z. Behav Res Ther 2023;165:104308
key_trials.design: Three-level meta-analysis, 33 RCTs, with trial sequential analysis
key_trials.finding: Post-treatment g=0.44 pain intensity, 0.59 physical function, 0.43 depression; face-to-face > internet; larger in headache/fibromyalgia; effects decline with longer follow-up

key_trials.citation: Ma TW, Yuen AS, Yang Z. Clin J Pain 2023;39:147-157
key_trials.finding: SMD -0.88 pain-related functioning, -0.45 pain intensity, -0.74 depression; larger vs waitlist/usual care

key_trials.citation: Hughes LS et al. Clin J Pain 2017;33:552-568
key_trials.design: Meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (mostly vs no treatment/TAU)
key_trials.finding: Small-medium effects on functioning, anxiety, depression; pain intensity and QoL n.s.; possible overestimation from methodological limits

controversy: Critics say 'acceptance' can feel like resignation or can imply that pain is psychological. ACT was drawn into the NICE NG193 backlash, in which the Faculty of Pain Medicine and the British Pain Society objected to the drug de-recommendations. Cochrane 2020 rated the ACT evidence 'very low quality', which contrasts with the positive later meta-analyses. Those meta-analyses themselves note allegiance concerns, waitlist/TAU-dominated designs and larger effects against weak controls. Head-to-head trials against CBT (Wetherell 2011) and applied relaxation (Kemani 2015) show broadly similar outcomes. Mediation results are mixed, and some question whether ACT is distinct from CBT. PRT/EAET proponents argue ACT under-targets pain-danger beliefs. Stanza's trials were sponsor-funded, used unmasked staff and a symptom-tracking control, and had PGIC as the primary endpoint. FDA authorization preceded publication of the phase 3 trial.

popularity.reach_estimate: Roughly 10^5.5-10^6 people with chronic pain have received ACT for pain cumulatively. This is an order-of-magnitude guess based on several thousand trial participants, ~20 years of routine use in NHS and US VA/academic pain services, internet programmes, Stanza users and self-help book sales. ACT across all conditions reaches far more people.
popularity.method_notes: The trajectory is anchored on documented milestones: the 1999 ACT manual; the 2005 pain books and Bath programme; the 2008 first pain process-outcome study; RCT accumulation (11 RCTs in the 2017 meta-analysis, 21-33 by 2023); NICE NG193 in 2021; Stanza's FDA De Novo in May 2023 and Lancet publication in 2024; and ACBS's count of 1,450+ RCTs in 2026. It reflects professional and research activity more than consumer social-media buzz, which is modest compared with consumer brain-retraining programmes. Reach is an order-of-magnitude guess, not a published figure. Added 2026-10-13: Hayes TEDx ~1.14M YouTube views; r/ChronicPain ~160-170K members (third-party tracker; Reddit API blocked). Book sales and Stanza user numbers are not published. Google Trends was not quantified.
